questions.q: In a QCNN, what plays the role of classical weight-sharing?
options: Applying the same parameterized two-qubit gate block to neighboring pairs of qubits across the register
Weight-sharing has no analogue anywhere in a QCNN
Measuring every qubit simultaneously at the first layer
Using a completely different random gate at every qubit position
questions.explain: Reusing the same trainable gate parameters across multiple qubit pairs is the direct structural analogue of a classical CNN filter's weight-sharing across spatial positions.

questions.q: Why is quantum 'pooling' NOT mathematically the same operation as classical max-pooling, even though both reduce active degrees of freedom?
options: Quantum pooling always increases the qubit count rather than reducing it
They are in fact mathematically identical operations, just applied to different data types
Classical pooling also requires an irreversible measurement, identical to quantum pooling

Classical max-pooling keeps the largest value from a neighborhood; quantum pooling measures (an irreversible, information-destroying operation) some qubits and conditionally acts on the rest -- a fundamentally different mechanism
questions.explain: The analogy between quantum and classical pooling is structural (both reduce active degrees of freedom layer by layer), not mechanistic -- quantum pooling involves measurement and conditional operations, nothing like picking a maximum value.

questions.q: What specific, legitimate result did Cong, Choi, and Lukin (2019) actually demonstrate for QCNNs?
options: QCNNs require no qubits at all, running entirely classically
QCNNs outperform classical CNNs on standard image classification benchmarks like ImageNet
QCNNs eliminate the need for any classical optimizer during training
QCNNs can efficiently recognize certain quantum error-correcting code phases and quantum many-body phases of matter -- a task about classifying quantum data, not classical images
questions.explain: The original QCNN result is specifically about classifying quantum data (phases of matter, error-correcting code phases) -- a real, useful, narrow result, not a claim about classical image classification.

questions.q: What is wrong with the reasoning 'QCNNs are the quantum version of CNNs, so they should be at least as good at image classification'?
options: The proven QCNN result is about classifying quantum data (output of a quantum system), not classical images; no application to classical datasets has demonstrated a practical advantage over classical CNNs
Nothing is wrong -- this reasoning is exactly correct and well-supported by evidence
QCNNs cannot process any kind of data at all, quantum or classical
Classical CNNs have been proven mathematically incapable of image classification
questions.explain: The 'quantum version of X' framing conflates two different task domains -- the genuinely proven QCNN result applies to quantum-native data, and applying the architecture to classical images has not shown any demonstrated advantage over classical CNNs.

questions.q: What does the classical CNN property of 'locality' refer to, as the baseline this lesson compares QCNNs against?
options: A property unique to quantum circuits with no classical analogue
The requirement that all training data come from one geographic location
The fact that CNNs can only run on local hardware, never in the cloud
A filter processes only a small, local neighborhood of the input (e.g., a small image patch) at each application, rather than the whole input at once
questions.explain: Locality means a convolutional filter looks at a small local region of the input at a time (e.g., a 3x3 pixel patch), which combined with weight-sharing across positions gives CNNs their efficiency and translation invariance.
